name: Embedded Chat
tagline: A drop-in group chat widget you paste into your own site so visitors can talk to each other in real time.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The chat itself is one of the most well trodden tutorials in software: a websocket server, a message table, a scrolling list, done in an afternoon. What you are actually buying is everything bolted around that loop: hosted sockets that stay up when 400 people pile in, moderation and ban tooling, spam and abuse filtering, presence, and a widget that renders politely inside somebody else's CSS. For a small site with a few dozen friendly users, a self-hosted version is genuinely fine and will cost you a few dollars of VPS. For anything public and anonymous, you will spend your second weekend writing a rate limiter and your third weekend deleting slurs by hand. Build it if the audience is known, pay if the audience is the internet.
coreLoopDIY: Runs a websocket chat room with persisted history, nicknames, and a one line embed script you can drop into any page.
requirements: A small always-on server or VPS, since websockets do not love serverless
A domain or subdomain with TLS so the widget can embed on https pages
Somewhere to put a SQLite file that survives restarts
whatYouLose: Hosted socket infrastructure that absorbs traffic spikes without you watching a dashboard
Moderation tooling: bans, mutes, word filters, reporting, audit trails
Abuse and spam defence, which is the real cost of any anonymous public chat
Mobile push and email notifications for messages you missed
Any AI layer: summaries, auto moderation, assistant replies in the room
moatNotes: The hard part was never the chat loop, it is staying online and keeping the room habitable while you sleep.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a chat room is a liability as much as a feature. The moment it is public, it attracts spam bots, link farms and the kind of user who tests whether you built a word filter, and a hosted product has already fought that fight across thousands of sites. Add the operational reality that websockets need a process that never dies, and the fact that the widget has to look correct inside every badly written stylesheet on the web, and a few dollars a month starts looking cheaper than owning an uptime pager for a comment box.
notes: Weekend one is the fun part, weekend two is the rate limiter. Budget for weekend two.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted embeddable group chat, single repo, no accounts and no third party services.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20, TypeScript, Express for HTTP, the ws package for websockets.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for persistence, file path from DATA_PATH in .env.
- No React. The widget is a single vanilla TS file bundled with esbuild into one small IIFE.

Server:
- POST-less API, state lives on the socket. Endpoints: GET /embed.js serving the bundled widget, GET /api/history?room=ID returning the last 100 messages, and a /ws websocket endpoint.
- Messages table: id, room, nickname, body, created_at, ip_hash. Hash IPs with a salt from .env, never store raw IPs.
- On connect the client sends {room, nickname}; server joins it to an in-memory room map and streams new messages to everyone in that room.
- Rate limit: max 5 messages per 10 seconds per socket, max 1000 chars per message, reject and send an error frame rather than silently dropping.
- Simple blocklist: words loaded from blocklist.txt at boot, matched messages are rejected with a reason.
- Admin: if ADMIN_TOKEN from .env is passed as a query param on the socket, allow delete-message and ban-ip-hash frames.

Widget:
- Renders into a div with data-room and data-embedded-chat attributes, all styles inlined in a shadow root so the host page CSS cannot touch it.
- Nickname prompt stored in localStorage, scrolling message list, textarea, enter to send, auto reconnect with backoff.
- Shows a connection state pill and the current room member count.

Explicitly out of scope: file uploads, threads, reactions, mobile push, email notifications, AI moderation, private DMs, OAuth.

Deliver a README with the embed snippet to paste, a .env.example with DATA_PATH, IP_SALT, ADMIN_TOKEN and PORT, and a docker-compose.yml with a named volume for the database. Add a load test script using autocannon-style socket spam so I can see where it falls over before my users do.
